newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FEATURE-Latin American red tape ties you up, ties you down.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Latin American red tape ties you up, ties you down.

text.p: Hyper-inflation used to be Latin America's public enemy No. 1 but today there is a new group of villains: the pernicious paper clip, the vile government form and the evil rubber stamp.
In a dank office in Caracas, a functionary yawned the other day and pointed a manicured finger at a hand-written note tacked to her battered grill. "No paper," she repeated.

The boredom, red fingernails and sign were Venezuelan. But the Catch-22 conundrum -- a government bureaucracy run out of the very paper it legally requires -- could have been repeated nearly anywhere in the region as Latin American governments move to streamline, straighten out, rationalise and re-jig their corrupt and often surreal bureaucracies.

The aim? To pour a quart from a pint pot by improving public services despite tight spending limits imposed by the region's recent, tough free market reforms. "The whole issue of bureaucracy is related to the need to improve efficiency in public spending," Jose Rutman, an economist at Argentina's Broda Group, said.

The upside is great; the downside rimmed with peril. "The inefficiency, the corruption of functionaries, their venality ... is our democracies' greatest threat," Venezuelan Foreign Minister Miguel Angel Burelli Rivas warned recently.

Burelli has promised concrete solutions from the Seventh Ibero-American Summit to be held in Venezuela this September. One of six workshops will cover ethics and public administration, another the administration of justice.
ADMINISTRATION - A FAR AWAY GOAL
"Unfortunately, in our countries we more often speak of non- administration," Burelli said.

In Venezuela, the court system moves so slowly the accused often finish their sentences before going to trial, and in one recent Brazilian court ruling state-owned Banco do Brasil was ordered to pay $250 million for mistakenly bouncing a $60 check. Even the church is guilty of bureaucratic obfuscation, turning at least one Colombian wedding into a confusion of red tape rather than a celebration with white lace.
"It's a kind of inquisitorial, control-freak mentality," Caracas-based political consultant Erik Ekvall said.

Every Latin American has blanched at the word "notary" and known the frustration of standing in an interminable line only to be told: come back tomorrow. But it is the public purse rather than public complaints that prompted most reform moves.

When Colombian president Ernesto Samper banned rubber stamps from public offices as part of a 1995 anti-corruption drive, he noted a World Bank report that estimated businessmen waste 10 percent of their time and 12 percent of their employees' time complying with government regulations.

In Brazil, bureaucracy is blamed for the "Custo Brazil" or "Brazil cost." During May's $3 billion auction of state mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD), the government had to notarize thousands of legal papers before a court would consider overturning an injunction blocking the sale.
As the world waited and the credibility of the government's economic plan balanced on a knife-edge, the notary's work meant an extra day's delay.
Ecuador's state payroll takes-up some 40 percent of the national budget, reducing funds available for investment, Quito Construction Chamber chief Hernan Mejia said.
WHEN EMPLOYEES ARE WHITE ELEPHANTS

And in Venezuela, whose 1.4 million state employees have been called by Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff "a tangle, a white elephant," the definition of corruption has been expanded to include inefficiency and maladministration.

"When the state cannot produce an identity card ... when permits or documents don't make it through a notary or court without a facilitating payment ... when the National Pantheon is falling down for lack of maintenance ... this is corruption," fumed Venezuelan Comptroller Eduardo Roche Lander in his annual corruption report.
Chilean historian Claudio Veliz put the blame on the colonial years when the Spanish empire was as firmly bound by voluminous laws to Madrid as the orbits of planets to the sun.

"There was an accepted notion, it sounds silly now, called the Conscience of the King whereby he would literally be dammed if any crime, sin, cruelty or injustice was committed in the Indies due to a legislative omission," he told Reuters in telephone interview from Boston University. The result was a proliferation of rules and regulations encompassing every facet of life from trade to officially approved names for children, as is still the case in Argentina.

"The difference between the letter of the law and its application was huge," Veliz said. That breach continues today. "There remains this faith that noble laws will produce noble behaviour," he added.
Add an underpaid, overstaffed civil service to the mix and the Byzantine brew is an invitation for administrative discretion and graft that often works against those it is designed to help.
Can the old, control-freak mind-set be dismantled? "Very difficult," Veliz replied. "Historically speaking it was very successful, at least until yesterday."

Cuba, where "socioismo" or buddyism, a pun on socialism, is used to lubricate the wheels of officialdom, continues to resist the regional trend. But free market reforms and trade liberalisation have eroded much of the Latin American state's traditionally centralized power.

"Industrialists in Peru devoted 30 to 40 percent of their time during the past 25 years chasing government officers ... to import and export, sell and buy foreign exchange and get permits," prominent Peruvian businessman Jorge Gruenberg said.
"It's not so now. Since this government (President Alberto Fujimori's) I haven't been to the ministry in six years."
Brazil is trying to push through civil service reforms and laws that would privatise much of the public sector. So too Argentina in its Second Reform of the State.
